title: What is Base64? How Base64 encoding works, with examples — cv.cm
description: Base64 turns binary data into 64 safe text characters, 3 bytes into 4. See how "Man" becomes TWFu, why output is 33% larger, and where Base64 is used.
answer: Base64 is a way to represent binary data using only 64 printable characters: A–Z, a–z, 0–9, + and /, with = as padding. It splits every 3 bytes into four 6-bit groups and maps each group to one character, so "Man" becomes "TWFu". It makes binary data safe for text-only channels such as email, JSON and URLs, at the cost of about 33% more size. It is an encoding, not encryption.

sections.h: How Base64 works, step by step
body: Base64 is defined in RFC 4648. Because 64 = 2⁶, each output character carries exactly 6 bits, and 3 bytes (24 bits) map neatly onto 4 characters.

ol: Look each up in the alphabet (0 = A, 25 = Z, 26 = a, 51 = z, 52 = 0, 61 = 9, 62 = +, 63 = /): T, W, F, u.

body: When the input length is not a multiple of 3, the last group is filled with zero bits and `=` marks the missing bytes, so the output length is always a multiple of 4.
Encoded length is `4 × ceil(n ÷ 3)` characters for n bytes. A 1 MB file becomes about 1.33 MB of text, and MIME email adds line breaks every 76 characters, pushing the overhead slightly higher.

ul: Email attachments: MIME encodes files as Base64 because the original mail system carried only 7-bit text.
Data URLs: small images inlined in HTML or CSS, written as `data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo...`.
JSON and XML APIs that need to carry binary data such as images, keys or certificates.
JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), whose header and payload are Base64url-encoded JSON.
PEM files for TLS certificates and keys, which wrap Base64 between `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` lines.
HTTP Basic authentication, which sends `username:password` Base64-encoded.

body: Inlining images as data URLs saves a network request but adds 33% to their size and prevents separate caching, so it is usually worthwhile only for very small images.

sections.h: Base64 vs Base64url and other encodings
body: Standard Base64 uses `+` and `/`, which have special meaning in URLs and file names. The URL-safe variant in the same RFC replaces them with `-` and `_` and often omits the `=` padding.

body.note: Base64 is not encryption. Anyone can decode it instantly, so a Base64 password or API key in a URL, config file or JWT payload is effectively plain text.

ul: Text must be converted to bytes first, normally as UTF-8. In JavaScript, `btoa()` throws an error on characters outside Latin-1 such as emoji or Chinese unless the string is UTF-8-encoded first.
Mixing the standard and URL-safe alphabets causes decode errors; replace `-` and `_` with `+` and `/` before using a standard decoder.
Missing padding can make strict decoders fail; add `=` until the length is a multiple of 4.
Line breaks from email-style encoding must be removed before some decoders accept the string.

faq.q: Why does Base64 make data bigger?
faq.a: Every 3 bytes become 4 characters, and each character is stored as a full byte, so the output is about 33% larger than the input.
No. It hides nothing; decoding requires no key. Use real encryption such as AES to protect data, and Base64 only to transport the result as text.

faq.q: What does the = at the end of Base64 mean?
faq.a: It is padding. One `=` means the last group held 2 bytes, and `==` means it held only 1 byte.

faq.q: How do I recognize a Base64 string?
faq.a: It contains only letters, digits, + and / (or - and _), its length is usually a multiple of 4, and it may end in one or two = signs. Strings starting with `eyJ` are often Base64-encoded JSON, because JSON text beginning with `{"` encodes to a string beginning with `eyJ`.
